claims.text: A continuous, dense spinel-type oxide film governs the coupled tribocorrosion response of high-entropy alloys.
The governing oxide film is enriched in oxide-forming elements such as Al and Fe.
The oxide film limits ion penetration and thereby reduces corrosion.
The oxide film acts as a wear-resistant layer and reduces material removal.
The initial alloy has a multiphase microstructure produced by powder metallurgy.
Conventional processing of the alloy yields only a limited or discontinuous oxide layer.
Higher sintering or thermal exposure can promote a robust, continuous spinel oxide film.
Compositional tuning can enrich the surface in oxide-forming elements and promote the spinel film.
The proposed response occurs during simultaneous wear and corrosion in an electrolyte such as 3.5 wt% NaCl at elevated temperature.
Frictional local heating is sufficient to drive formation of the oxide film.
The oxide barrier changes corrosion from direct attack to diffusion-controlled degradation.
The oxide is a robust, low-friction layer that resists mechanical removal.
An oxide-promoted alloy will have lower total degradation than a matched baseline lacking a continuous oxide film.
The oxide-promoted alloy will exhibit lower corrosion current density than the baseline.
The oxide-promoted alloy will exhibit lower wear depth than the baseline.
The prediction should hold when oxidants and friction-induced heating are sufficient to form and maintain the film.
The prediction may fail when mechanical removal is faster than oxide-film reformation.
The prediction may fail in oxygen-deficient environments.
Protective in situ oxide films have previously been observed separately in corrosion and high-temperature wear studies.
Failure to obtain statistically significant reductions in both corrosion current density and wear depth is defined as falsifying the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The experiment is described as comparing two sets of the same alloy, but it also permits compositional adjustment and a baseline lacking sufficient oxide-forming elements. Changing composition would make the samples compositionally unmatched and prevent isolation of oxide-film continuity as the sole cause.
The rule treats failure to observe the promoted film as falsification of the film mechanism, although that result could instead mean that the intervention failed to create the proposed mediator.
